content: Intubation in newborns is associated with bacterial colonization of the respiratory tract, which may increase the risk of developing infections. Such infections can prolong the need for mechanical ventilation and elevate the likelihood of chronic lung disease. To mitigate these risks, the use of prophylactic antibiotics has been proposed for all mechanically ventilated newborns. However, there is concern that the potential harms of this approach may outweigh its benefits. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of prophylactic antibiotics on mortality and morbidity in intubated, ventilated newborns who are not known to have an infection. Two specific policies regarding the use of prophylactic antibiotics were examined: 1. For newborns intubated for mechanical ventilation, the use of prophylactic antibiotics throughout the duration of intubation was compared to placebo or no treatment. 2. For intubated, ventilated newborns who were started on antibiotics at the time of intubation but whose initial cultures were negative for sepsis, the continuation of antibiotics was compared to discontinuation. The search for relevant studies included databases such as MEDLINE (from January 1950 to March 2007), CINAHL (from 1982 to March 2007), the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (Issue 1, 2007), the Cochrane Neonatal Group Specialised Register, and reference lists of articles. This search was updated in November 2010. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials of sufficient quality, where mechanically ventilated newborns were randomized to receive prophylactic antibiotics versus placebo or no treatment. Two reviewers independently assessed the quality of the trials. Two studies met the inclusion criteria for this review. One study was of insufficient quality to draw any meaningful conclusions. The other study, which was of fair quality, did not find significant differences between the treatment and control groups in any of the reported outcomes. However, it is important to note that the rates of septicaemia were not reported in this study. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence from randomized trials to either support or refute the use of prophylactic antibiotics at the initiation of mechanical ventilation in newborns. Similarly, there is insufficient evidence to support or refute the continuation of antibiotics once initial cultures have ruled out infection in mechanically ventilated newborns.
